items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: none of the greatest musicians I ever talked to, let me say the Dodds or Simeon or any of those that worked with him

ctx.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to…
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Also, Omer Simeon, who was certainly one of the outstanding New Orleans clarinetists

ctx.x: Well, you think that maybe it has something to do with the general environment.

Or else it's the type of people that, for one thing, one of the great principles which you can't really overemphasize in New Orleans music, in the jazz, is the working together. The way they can work together. They're all there to help one another, as they say. They'll, they're not there to steal the spotlight. They're always there trying to help somebody misses a note or they can see they're falling down on their part. They'll put in notes that'll fill in or they'll, I mean, it's not quite that simple, but I…
He was my favorite of all of them on my own record.
